title: Dad questions Taser use; 'He wasn't an angel but does that justify killing him?';
article: The father of the man who died after being Tasered by Norfolk OPP Monday morning is questioning the police's need to use the weapon.
Jeffery Mark Marreel, 36, who occasionally lived with his parents in the Delhi area, was known to police and had a history of drug abuse, said his father, Noel Marreel.
"He wasn't an angel but does that justify killing him?"
Marreel asked Tuesday.
"Was it necessary to Taser him?
I just don't think so."
Marreel said two officers informed him of his son's death Monday afternoon but did not say he was Tasered.
"I found out on the radio and that is one hell of a way to find out,' Marreel said.
"It just doesn't make sense how so much time passed after being Tasered and when he died."
Norfolk OPP responded to a report of an unwanted man in Fisher's Glen, south of Simcoe, Monday morning.
Police found Marreel, who was described as "combative" in a news release, and used a stun gun to subdue him.
Marreel was arrested and taken to the Norfolk OPP detachment in Simcoe, where he collapsed.
Officers administered first aid until an ambulance arrived.
He died at Norfolk General Hospital in Simcoe.
Ontario's Special Investigations Unit is probing the incident, since Marreel died in police custody.
Noel Marreel described his son as a big, strong man weighing about 200 pounds.
"But he's been arrested before and he's always gone quietly, never resisted," he said.
"I just don't understand why?
Are the police that poorly trained to have a death like this?"
Jeffrey Marreel's death is the 21st in Canada relating to Taser use and further fuels questions about police use of the supposedly non-lethal weapon.
"It's too late for my boy but I'm sure there will be many more," Marreel said.
Amnesty International is calling for the use of stun guns to be suspended because of the lack of independent testing on the weapon's effects.
"Particularly in vulnerable groups like the mentally ill or drug and alcohol abusers," said Hilary Homes, security and human rights campaigner with the group's Canadian chapter.
"Testing has just begun on the effects of Tasers on these individuals."
Homes said that, normally with use of force, studies are conducted, then the weapon is given to officers.
"But with Tasers, it's been the other way around," she said in a telephone interview.
"Only now are more tests and studies being done."
A report released last week on RCMP Taser use noted the these vulnerable groups are more likely to be Tasered.
The report also said the RCMP have been using them increasingly every year since their introduction in Canada in 2001.
"They call it usage creep," Homes said.
"I do believe they can be a useful tool for police with imminent threat and standoff situations, but there's an increase in use and they are using them earlier in situations and multiple times.
There just isn't enough information about their effects for police to use them responsibly."
Norfolk OPP acquired two Tasers in 2005.
Peter Hellyer, chairman of Norfolk's police services board, said Taser use has always been a concern of the board's and is even more so now that there is a death.
Still, he said he's confident that local OPP do not misuse the weapons.
"Only a selected and very experienced sergeants and emergency response team members are trained to use a Taser," Hellyer said.
"They are the only ones that use them and, to my knowledge, we don't have very many."
He added Tasers have been used successfully in Norfolk, referring to an incident in August 2006 where police used a Taser to subdue a man who was wielding a sword and axe.
Hellyer said he does not want to prejudge this week's case.
"When all is said and done it is regrettable," he said.
An autopsy of Marreel's body was done Tuesday but an SIU spokesperson said more forensic tests need to be completed before determining a cause of death.
